Paleomagnetism of the Late Cretaceous volcanic rocks of the
Shimaoshan Group in Yongtai County, Fujian Province
HUANG Sheng1,2, PAN YongXin3 & ZHU RiXiang1*
1 State Key Laboratory of Lithospheric Evolution, Institute of Geology and Geophysics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 100029, China;
2 Graduate University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 100049, China;
3 Key Laboratory of the Earth’s Deep Interior, Institute of Geology and Geophysics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 100029, China
Received March 2, 2012, accepted August 2, 2012; published online October 12, 2012
It has been debated whether there was southward movement of the South China Block (SCB) during the Cretaceous. In this
study, a paleomagnetic investigation was carried out on the Late Cretaceous volcanic rocks (~88 Ma) of the Shimaoshan Group
in Yongtai County, Fujian Province. Rock magnetic experiments showed that magnetite in pseudo-single-domain and
multi-domain grain and hematite were predominant magnetic phases. Stepwise thermal demagnetization successfully isolated
characteristic directional components at high-temperature interval (> 500°C) from 383 specimens in 19 sites, which yielded a
paleomagnetic pole for the studied section at 83.1°N, 152.6°E (N = 19, A = 3.9°), and the scatter S = 9.0. The Fisher distri-
95 B
bution of virtual geomagnetic poles (VGPs) and the consistence of S with the expected value at the 95% confidence level in-
B
dicate that the yielded paleomagnetic pole is free of paleomagnetic secular variation influence. The new pole, which is well
consistent with that from the Eurasian apparent polar wander path (APWP) curve, suggests no obvious southward movement
of the sampling site during the Cretaceous.
South China Block, Late Cretaceous, volcanic rock, paleomagnetic secular variation, paleomagnetic pole

To probe the discrepancy between red beds, we reex-
amined the red-beds paleomagnetic results in SCB with
more strict criteria: (1) In order to avoid the influence of
tectonic movement, the sampling areas undergoing the local
deformation were excluded. For example, in the western
part of SCB, only the combined paleomagnetic pole (72.8°N,
241.1°E, A = 6.3, N = 16) from Guanyin section (N = 7)
95
and Feixianguan section (N = 9) in Sichuan Province was
retained, where the pole from the Feixianguan section was
corrected by 8° of local rotations [12, 15]. (2) Only the data
from Late Cretaceous were discussed. (3) The amount of
sampling sites must be greater than 5. The data satisfying
the criteria above are listed in Table 2.
Based on the paleomagnetic poles from red beds, the
mean paleomagnetic poles for the middle-western and east-
ern part of SCB in the Late Cretaceous (the pole from
Mayuan basin was excluded in calculation) were 73.0°N,
